Currently, many independent workshops must turn away customers because they lack access to the proprietary information needed to service modern, increasingly computerized vehicles.
The proposal draws inspiration from Australia's 2022 right-to-repair legislation, which reportedly made independent mechanic repairs about 25 percent cheaper on average than dealership services. Beyond repair access, the policy package includes consumer protections for car purchases: eliminating hidden finance commissions at dealerships, allowing penalty-free cancellations within two weeks of purchase, and requiring clearer upfront pricing. Additional measures focus on fuel affordability, including freezing fuel tax increases and exploring options for unmanned petrol stations on surplus government land.
This story touches on a quiet shift happening across industries—the tension between manufacturers' proprietary control and consumers' ownership rights. As cars become more like computers on wheels, the question of who can access their inner workings has real financial consequences for everyday drivers. It's a reminder that ownership in the modern age increasingly means fighting for the right to truly control what we've paid for, whether that's fixing our own devices or choosing an affordable local mechanic over a distant dealership.

item.title: Trio of teachers takes pride in being poll workers at Juiz de Fora's largest polling station
item.description:
On election day in Juiz de Fora, Brazil, democracy revealed itself not through grand institutions but through the quiet dedication of ordinary citizens. At Colégio Jesuítas, the city's largest polling station serving over 8,000 voters across 25 sections, stories of civic participation unfolded in unexpected ways.
Three teachers—Alessandra Valestina Matos de Abreu, Noiaras Menezes Rosa, and Silvânia Batista Clemente—have turned poll work into both tradition and friendship. For three elections running, they've volunteered together as poll workers, viewing their Sunday service as an expression of citizenship and a way to help others exercise their democratic rights. What began as civic duty evolved into something more meaningful: a shared bond and a commitment to future generations. "We have to think not just about today, but about what comes ahead, the future—for young people, children, grandchildren," Noiara explained.
Meanwhile, parents Larissa and Thiago brought their two young children along to vote, transforming the polling station into a classroom. Their six-year-old daughter already knows the names of presidents and candidates, beginning to grasp the competing ideas at stake. Even their two-year-old is being introduced to this civic ritual. For this family, voting is teaching by example—showing their children they're part of building the country's future before they're old enough to cast ballots themselves. It's a reminder that democracy lives not only in laws and institutions, but in these small acts of participation, passed down like precious knowledge from one generation to the next.

item.title: There are only six of these trees left in the wild. Conservationists are cloning them
item.description:
Deep in the forests just south of Canberra, six ancient eucalyptus trees represent the last survivors of an ice-age species. The Eucalyptus recurva, known as the Mongarlowe mallee or ice-age gum, is so rare that only a handful of people have ever laid eyes on it. The largest specimens are estimated to be between 3,000 and 6,000 years old, their survival spanning millennia while the world around them transformed.
Conservationists face a delicate challenge: the six remaining trees are too far apart to naturally reproduce, and they produce no wild seeds. Over decades, teams from the Australian National Botanic Gardens and NSW's Saving Our Species program have been painstakingly cloning the trees by grafting wild cuttings onto hybrid rootstock. They've successfully created multiple copies of four of the six wild plants, establishing a crucial insurance population. The next hurdle is even more intricate—getting the cloned trees to flower and produce genetically pure seeds. Flowering is unpredictable and can take up to twenty years, with individual trees blooming at different times. The team is experimenting with growth regulators while preparing to hand-pollinate the flowers and protect them from insects that might introduce pollen from other eucalyptus species, creating unwanted hybrids.
This story offers a glimpse into the patient, meticulous work of conservation—a reminder that saving a species sometimes means committing to a project that will outlast careers and span generations. It's a quiet testament to the determination of people who refuse to let Australia's rarest eucalyptus slip into extinction without a fight.

item.title: How a high school student became Portrait Artist of the Year
item.description:
When Jasmine 'Jazz' Lancaster Merton skipped her Year 12 camp to compete in Australia's Portrait Artist of the Year, she assumed she'd simply meet some fellow art enthusiasts and head home. Instead, the 17-year-old from North Sydney found herself painting her way through rounds featuring Casey Donovan, Marcia Hines, and INXS's Kirk Pengilly—ultimately winning the entire competition. Her prize: a commission to paint entertainer Justine Clarke for the National Portrait Gallery, a remarkable honor for someone still navigating high school assignments.
Jazz's bedroom doubles as her studio, and portraits have become her obsession. She's drawn to the infinite ways people customize themselves, the endless variations of human faces. Her passion earned early validation when her self-portrait won the Young Archies prize in 2025, but nothing prepared her for the pressure of balancing a nationally televised commission with looming school deadlines. With her school's support, she managed both, working through what she describes with characteristic warmth as "a bit of a priorities call" between a life-changing opportunity and her university entrance exams.
What makes Jazz's story quietly remarkable isn't just her technical skill with colored pencils and oils, but her grounded perspective on sudden recognition. She speaks of staring at Justine Clarke's face for weeks with humor rather than hubris, and admits she's still adjusting to sharing something so personal with TV crews and gallery crowds. For anyone who's ever wondered whether youthful passion can find its footing in the professional world, Jazz's journey from bedroom studio to national gallery offers a gentle, encouraging answer.

item.title: "Once you see her, you can't stop thinking about her": Ana Mendieta, the artist who defied limits with her body and whose mysterious death continues to divide the art world
item.description:
Ana Mendieta created art that merged her body with the earth, leaving impressions in soil, arranging flowers in caves, and working with blood, gunpowder, and natural materials across forests and rivers. Born in Cuba in 1948, she was sent to the United States at age twelve during the Revolution, spending formative years separated from her parents in Iowa orphanages and foster homes. That profound displacement shaped sixteen years of striking artistic expression that blurred boundaries between performance, sculpture, and the landscape itself.
For decades, Mendieta remained relatively unknown to general audiences, though deeply admired by fellow artists. Her work posed practical challenges: how do you collect or preserve art designed to return to nature? The ephemeral quality that made her creations so powerful also meant they existed primarily through documentation—photographs and films of moments already passed. Her tragic death in 1985, falling from a 34th-floor window in circumstances that remain disputed, complicated her legacy further. Some feel the controversy surrounding her husband's trial overshadowed her artistic achievements, reducing her to a victim rather than celebrating her as a creator.
Now, major exhibitions like the one at London's Tate Modern are introducing Mendieta to wider audiences, revealing an artist who literally and figuratively left her mark on contemporary art. Her work carries a curious magnetism—once encountered, it lingers in the mind. This story matters because it recovers a visionary who transformed personal displacement into art that connected human presence with the natural world, and because it asks how we remember artists whose most profound statements were written in sand, ash, and time.

item.title: Ethiopian rebel forces withdraw from Tigray regional capital
item.description:
Ethiopian rebel forces from the Tigray People's Liberation Front have temporarily withdrawn from Mekelle, the regional capital of Tigray, as federal government troops and allied forces advance toward the city. The TPLF stated the withdrawal was intended to protect civilians, while residents confirmed that pro-government forces now control Mekelle and mobile phone services have partially resumed.
This development represents a significant shift in a conflict that has reignited after a fragile peace. Fighting between the TPLF and federal forces has flared in recent weeks across Ethiopia's northern regions, raising international alarm about regional stability. The unrest comes barely two years after a devastating civil war ended with an African Union-brokered peace agreement in 2022—a conflict estimated to have claimed 600,000 lives and pushed Tigray to the brink of famine. Relations between the parties have deteriorated over the past six months, with mutual accusations of violating the peace deal. Last month, the TPLF joined six other armed groups, including the Fano militia, in an alliance aimed at removing Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government.
The conflict's ripples are spreading beyond Ethiopia's borders. The country has severed diplomatic ties with Eritrea over alleged support for rebels and expelled an Egyptian diplomat on similar accusations, prompting reciprocal expulsions. The United Nations has warned that renewed fighting is severely hampering humanitarian efforts in a region still recovering from catastrophic losses. This story matters because it chronicles not just the fragility of hard-won peace, but the human cost when reconciliation unravels—and the quiet courage of civilians caught between forces beyond their control.
